question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The paper describes researchers designing prototype AR interactions and two AR apps primarily to demonstrate accessible alternatives to common AR tasks, derived from a taxonomy of constituent tasks in existing apps. The work is framed around making AR tasks accessible (utility) rather than around fun or entertainment, and design decisions were not made via participatory fun-focused workshops. This aligns best with a mostly utility-first design where primary utilitarian mechanics (accessible interaction patterns) are designed first, with no strong indication of clinician-only development or later-added fun.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: Participants complete a fixed sequence of clearly specified AR tasks with explicit instructions and success conditions (e.g., scan four surfaces totaling five square meters, place objects at prompted locations, follow guided narration). Interaction follows app-defined mechanics with little freedom or house-rule style modification, aligning best with a rigid-rules game structure.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: Tasks involve scanning surfaces, placing and locating virtual objects, arranging furniture, and exploring an educational solar system app. Outcomes are fully determined by participants’ actions and understanding of instructions; there is no randomization affecting success beyond object placement for the experimenter. This is an interaction/usability study, not a game of chance, so the design is entirely skill-based.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely solo (i.e., solitaire),
        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),
        (3) mix of solo and social affordances (i.e., animal crossing),
        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),
        (5) entirely social (i.e., tag)
reasoning: The study involved individual blind participants using AR prototypes alone in a room to complete predefined tasks (scanning surfaces, placing and locating virtual objects, arranging furniture, and exploring an educational solar system app). There is no mention of multiplayer, co-present players, or social interaction mechanics; all tasks are single-user interactions with the system, so the design is entirely solo.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The study involves single users completing AR tasks (scanning surfaces, then placing objects, then searching, then arranging furniture, then using an educational app). Interactions are structured as guided, sequential steps (e.g., step-by-step placement, guided narration), not simultaneous or multi-actor, and not free-timing within a shared turn. This best matches a design that follows a set of steps rather than turn-based or simultaneous play.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The study involves single-user mobile AR prototypes used by blind participants in a lab, with tasks like scanning surfaces, placing and locating virtual objects, and exploring educational content. There is no mention of multiple users, real-time opponents, or time pressure; interactions are between a single user and the app at their own pace. This aligns best with an entirely asynchronous design.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The study involves single users interacting with accessible AR prototypes (retail furniture app, educational solar system app, and constituent AR tasks) to complete scanning, placing, locating, arranging, and learning tasks. There is no mention of multiple players, opponents, or any competitive mechanics; the activities are purely about the user accomplishing tasks with the system, which best fits an entirely collaborative design.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The study is a single-user interaction evaluation of accessible AR prototypes (furniture and solar system apps) with blind participants using VoiceOver on iPhone. There are no multiple roles, teams, or differentiated abilities between participants; everyone uses the same interface and tasks. This corresponds most closely to an entirely symmetrical design among participants, even though it is not a competitive or cooperative game per se.
